# Trends in socioeconomic inequalities in self-rated health and mental distress during four decades in a Norwegian population: a HUNT Study

**Authors:** Hanne Dahl Vonen; Erik R Sund; Inger Ariansen; Steinar Krokstad

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Public Health and Nursing, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway | 2 Department of Public Health and Nursing, HUNT Research Centre, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Trondheim, Norway | 3 Levanger Hospital, Nord-Trøndelag Hospital Trust, Levanger, Norway | 4 Faculty of Nursing and Health Sciences, Nord University, Levanger, Norway | 5 Department of Chronic Diseases, The Norwegian Institute of Public Health, Oslo, Norway | 6 Department of Public Health and Nursing, HUNT Research Centre, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), Trondheim, Norway | 7 Levanger Hospital, Nord-Trøndelag Hospital Trust, Levanger, Norway

## Abstract

Socioeconomic inequalities constitute an important focus area for public health, and it has long been established that higher educational level and longer lifespan are correlated. Little is known about decennial time trends in poor self-rated health and mental distress.

This study linked decennial cross-sectional survey data on self-rated health and mental distress from the Trøndelag Health Study (HUNT) from 1984 to 2019 with educational registry data using personal identification numbers. Survey participation ranged from 50 807 to 77 212. Slope index of inequality (SII) and relative index of inequality (RII) were calculated using generalized linear models in Stata. Analyses were stratified by sex and age, using the age categories of 30–59 years and 60–80 years.

Absolute inequalities in self-rated health and mental distress between educational groups have stayed relatively stable throughout all rounds of HUNT. Relative inequalities in self-rated health and mental distress have generally increased, and both men and women with the lowest education level were more likely to experience poor self-rated health and mental distress relative to those with the highest education level. RII in self-rated health increased over time for both sexes and both age groups. RII for mental distress increased in both sexes and both age groups, except for men and women aged 60–80.

This study shows that relative inequalities in self-rated and mental health in the Norwegian population are still persistent and have increased. Further knowledge about groups with a disadvantageous health situation should have implications for health care resource allocation.

## Introduction

Those who have a higher educational status tend to live longer and healthier lives, illustrating the importance of social inequalities in public health. This phenomenon has been consistently observed in many countries, both in relation to somatic as well as mental health, and can thus be regarded as a pressing challenge.1,2 The reduction of health inequalities has therefore been an overarching political goal of the Norwegian state, which was manifested through the Law of Public Health in 2012. The overarching aim of this law was to contribute to societal development promoting health, hereby reducing health inequalities.3 There is a need to examine whether these goals have been achieved for key health measures in a country with a long-life expectancy.

Norway is a country that has an overall high standard of living, with a GDP per capita that is among the highest in The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) .4 It is known for having a strong health care system that is based, to a large extent, on a single-payer system. Health services are provided as a part of universal health and social insurance coverage, known as the National Insurance Scheme (NIS).5 On average, inhabitants tend to live long lives compared with the inhabitants of other OECD nations.4 However, despite a relatively high standard of health overall, wide health inequalities in Norway still persist, a phenomenon known as the Nordic paradox.6

Somatic health in terms of life expectancy and self-rated health has improved in the population during the past couple of decades.7 Self-rated mental health has seen a more uneven development, where the level of improvement depends on the age group in question.8 However, net health gains that have been achieved due to a higher standard of living and medical innovation have not been equally distributed across the population, which has led to increasing inequalities. Social inequalities in mortality in Norway have been extensively studied, with a great body of literature exploring the differences in mortality, health status and life expectancy across educational groups.9 While one study found increasing educational inequalities in expected lifetime in good health (as measured through questionnaires) and lifetime without long-standing limiting illness,7 another study found a strong increase in the relative inequalities in mortality in both men and women in the past decades.10

However, there has yet to be explored how self-rated health and symptoms of mental distress have developed among educational groups over the most recent decade, and how this compares with the development of the previous decades. As the subjective experience of a single diagnosis might vary between individuals, there is a need to look at how and the symptoms of ill health is affecting the perception of health status. Though self-rated health is a subjective health measure, it has been recognized as a very important health indicator11 and shown to be congruent with objective health parameters.12 Self-rated health is also a good way of taking into consideration heterogeneity in disease experience among individuals, and accounting for the added effects of disease interaction on one’s own health experience. As poor mental health may be hard to quantify as it tends to be underdiagnosed,13 this study uses symptoms of mental distress.

The aim of this study was to investigate how socioeconomic inequalities in self-rated health and mental distress have developed in a Norwegian population utilizing data from the Trøndelag Health Study (HUNT), from 1984–86 to 2017–19.

## Methods

This study used decennial cross-sectional survey data from the HUNT Study, which was linked to educational registry data. The data were linked by a third party using personal identification numbers, which is a unique number to each individual Norwegian resident.

The HUNT Study runs decennial comprehensive surveys which is supplemented by clinical examinations and biological samples. The HUNT-population is considered nationally representative.14 Four surveys have been completed, with the first round of HUNT1 being collected between 1984 and 1986, HUNT2 between 1995 and 1997, HUNT3 in 2006–08 and HUNT4 in 2017–19. The characteristics of the HUNT Study has been further described by Krokstad and colleagues.14,15

All adult (20+) inhabitants in the Nord-Trøndelag County were invited to participate in all surveys. HUNT1 included 77 212 participants and had an 89.4% response of all invited participants. HUNT2 included 65 237 participants with a 69.5% response of all invited participants. HUNT3 included 50 807 participants with a 54.1% response of all invited participants. HUNT4 included 56 042 participants with a 54.0% response.14,15

The study population was limited to participants from the age of 30 and up to the age of 80 at participation in the HUNT1-4 surveys. The lower age cut-off of 30 was established as this is an age by which we can assume that educational level will remain stable. The upper age cut-off of 80 was set due to falling participation beyond this age. Participants with missing values on education or belonged to the educational category trade school were excluded from the analysis, as this category of individuals was not sufficiently large for separate analysis.

Educational level was used as a proxy of socioeconomic status, utilizing data from the Norwegian National Education Database. Education was categorized as the highest educational level attained. Three educational categories were used, namely basic education (up to 10 years), secondary education (13 years) and university (16+). Education was used as it is stable over time, and widely recognized in the academic literature as a reliable measure of socioeconomic status.16 It is associated with other markers of socioeconomic status such as income and occupation.

Self-rated health was measured through the survey question ‘how is your health at the moment?’. The question had four answer options of ‘very good’, ‘good’, ‘fair’ and ‘poor’. For statistical analysis, these four answers were recreated as a dichotomous variable of good (corresponding to the answers of very good and good) and poor (corresponding to the answers of fair and poor).

Mental health status was captured through Cohort Norway Mental Health Index (CONOR-MHI). CONOR-MHI is considered to be a valid screening tool for mental distress in epidemiological research, and is highly correlated with other previously validated instruments measuring mental distress.17,18 The CONOR-MHI consists of a self-assessed questionnaire asking participants to rate from four different options ranging from ‘no’ to ‘very’, which were assigned the values 1–4, if they over the course of the last two weeks, felt seven different emotional states. These were ‘nervous and unsettled’, ‘troubled by anxiety’, ‘secure and calm’ (inverse score), ‘irritable’, ‘happy and optimistic’ (inverse score), ‘sad/depressed’ and ‘lonely’. The average CONOR-MHI score was calculated by dividing the total sum by seven. A CONOR-MHI score of ≥2.15 has commonly been used as a cut-off value for mental distress.19,20 CONOR-MHI was only available for the last three rounds of HUNT.

This paper is a sub-study in the project ‘A life-course approach to prevent noncommunicable diseases in an aging population—NCDNOR’, approved by the Regional Committee for Research Ethics South-east 2019/1203. NCDNOR is a research project aiming at establishing new knowledge in the prevention of noncommunicable diseases by combining noncommunicable disease endpoints across somatic disciplines, examining effects of socioeconomic circumstances, health behaviors, biological markers, and mental health throughout the life-course.21

### Statistical analysis

The analyses were performed in two age groups, 30–59 and 60–80 years, for men and women separately, and at each survey round. Educational inequalities in self-rated health and mental distress were measured using the relative index of inequality (RII) and the slope index of inequality (SII). These measures allow the adjustment of changes in the proportion with basic, secondary and university education over time. The percentage of participants with self-rated poor health and mental distress belonging to each educational group for each round of the HUNT survey is illustrated in Supplementary figure 2. Both are regression-based absolute and relative measures of inequalities in health, providing absolute and relative differences in the prevalence of outcomes between respondents with the lowest and highest educational level.22 Specifically, educational levels were assigned a ridit score ranging from 0 (the group with the highest level of education) to 1 (the group with the lowest level of education). The ridit score was based on the midpoint of the range in the cumulative distribution of the population of participants in the given educational category. We checked for linearity in the relationship between ridit score and self-rated health and mental distress graphically, and the linearity assumption seems to hold.

Both SII and RII were calculated using generalized linear models for the binomial family with identity and log link functions, respectively. Values of SII > 0 and RII > 1 indicate that the outcome is more prevalent among individuals with lower education than among individuals with higher education. The SII can be interpreted as prevalence differences, whereas the RII can be interpreted as prevalence ratios. SII and RII were obtained by separately regressing the outcomes on the ridit score. All models were adjusted for continuous age and estimated with 95% confidence intervals. Stata version 17 was used for all data management and analyses.

## Results

Table 1 shows how the educational composition of the HUNT-population has changed over the past decades, and that the general education level has increased for both men and women. Women included in the three last rounds of the study had higher education than men. The percentage of people reporting poor self-rated health decreased for both men and women in all four rounds of HUNT. A higher proportion of women reported poor self-rated health compared with men, and a slightly higher proportion reported mental distress. The total percentage of people with a CONOR-MHI above the cut-off value of 2.15 has been relatively stable over time for both men and women.

As can be seen in table 2, there were absolute and relative educational inequalities in self-rated health in both sexes and age categories in all study rounds. While the absolute inequalities in self-rated health between educational groups have stayed relatively similar throughout all rounds of HUNT from 1984 to 2019, they went numerically down for men and up for women in both age categories between HUNT3 and HUNT4. The exception was for women aged 30–59 years where absolute inequality in self-rated health increased over time (Supplementary figure 1). The relative inequality estimates in self-rated health have seen an overall increase since the first round of HUNT, for both men and women in both age groups. For women, this trend takes place from HUNT1 throughout HUNT4, for men from HUNT1 to HUNT3. This is further illustrated in figure 1. For women, relative inequalities increased numerically. For men, relative inequalities saw a slight numerical decrease between HUNT3 and HUNT4. However, men of lower education in the 30- to 59-year-old age category were still more than three times as likely to experience poor self-rated health in HUNT4 relative to men with high education in the same age group. In the 60- to 80-year-old age category, men of lower education were more than twice as likely to experience poor self-rated health relatively to the ones with higher education. In the last round of HUNT, the relative health inequalities between men and women were similar when comparing the two age categories. The results also show that the relative inequalities in self-rated health were higher among 30- to 59-year-olds than among 60- to 80-year-olds for both sexes.

For both men and women, there were absolute and relative educational inequalities in mental distress in both age categories in all study rounds. The absolute inequalities in mental distress have stayed relatively stable throughout the last three rounds of HUNT, except for women aged 60–80 years, where the absolute educational differences declined over time. Though absolute inequalities in mental distress have stayed more or less constant for both sexes, relative social inequalities increased numerically. The only exception is women aged 60–80, for which relative inequalities decreased between HUNT2 and HUNT3. As shown in table 3, relative inequalities in mental distress between the highest and lowest educational groups were similar between the sexes when comparing the two age categories. Both men and women with lowest education in the younger age category were more than three times as likely to experience mental distress relative to men and women with the highest education, whereas for the older age category, both men and women with the lowest education were between two and three times more likely to experience mental distress, relative to the ones with the highest education.

## Discussion

The results of this study show that absolute and relative social inequalities in poor self-rated health and mental distress are still persistent in this Norwegian population, and that relative inequalities are increasing for people aged 30–59 years old. This is despite wide political efforts to reduce health inequalities, both through implementing laws and through multiple political papers that have the aim of tackling this issue.

The origins of such inequalities might have several and complex explanations, as the mechanisms linking education as a proxy for socioeconomic status and health are not yet fully understood. There are, however, several plausible theories that attempt to explain the relationship between education and health, including that education affects income, employment status, occupation, health behaviors, and social factors and networks.23,24 When it comes to social inequalities in mental distress, differences in self-efficacy, social support and degree of economic problems have been proposed as explanatory mechanisms.25 Inequality itself has notably been regarded as a catalyst of ill health at national level, a phenomenon known as the Wilkinson hypothesis.26 This hypothesis postulates that it is, among other things, the lack of social trust and unequal distribution of resources that may generate unfavorable health outcomes in unequal societies.

Though Norway traditionally has been regarded as an egalitarian country when comparing it to other countries on a global level, relative inequalities in both income and wealth have increased over the past years.27 Due to the interconnected nature of inequalities and health outcomes, the increasing material inequalities in the Norwegian society might offer a partial explanation as to why relative health inequalities have overall seen an upward-facing trend over the past decades.9,10 Additionally, digitalization is increasingly shaping the structure and demands of labor markets, including the kinds of skills and competence that are necessary to obtain a job.28 Such restructuring might widen the health gap between educational groups as it may create larger income inequalities as well as increase the educational gap in the levels of employment.

The strength of this study includes that it covers a general unselected population in central region in Norway with a wide age range, utilize historical health data from the last four decades from a population shown to follow national health trends.14 Taking a subjective approach to health status allows for the analysis of actual experience of health and illness and is therefore a useful supplement to studies that look at differences in diagnoses and mortality. A large part of the burden of disease in Norway is characterized by diseases that does not necessarily cause immediate morbidity or mortality, but that still impacts quality of life, including mental disorders, lower back pain and headache disorders.29 Moreover, while the Norwegian public health strategy has proved successful in reducing health loss resulting from fatal diseases, there has not been an equal reduction in non-fatal health loss.29 To be able to reduce the prevalence of such factors, it is important to have knowledge of how the experience of illness is distributed along a social gradient in the population.

A limitation of the study is that the participation has been declining throughout the rounds of HUNT. A previous study found that non-participants in HUNT had lower socioeconomic status than those who participated and also poorer health.30 In terms of biasing the findings, the actual inequalities in health are likely larger than those observed. This may partly explain why the percentage of people who report poor self-rated health has decreased throughout the different HUNT studies. Additionally, the level of education has increased in the HUNT-population overall, as seen in table 1. As the group of people with the lowest level of education grows smaller, this may lead to a more selected group of people remaining in the low-education group, which may have a different health profile than the lower-educated group from previous decades. Moreover, it is important to note that the confidence intervals of the reported RII are relatively wide, indicating a certain lack of precision. However, as seen in figure 1, even at the lower ends of the confidence intervals, the RIIs show a difference in the estimated inequalities between the highest and lowest educational groups.

The findings of this study show that despite political efforts to reduce social inequalities in health, inequalities persist in the Norwegian society. Through legislation, the Norwegian authorities have succeeded in putting this important public health challenge on the agenda but have not succeeded in reducing the health differences. In our opinion, this is due to the lack of understanding the impact of underlying social determinants and the believe in that these inequalities can be reduces at municipality or individual levels. We observe unwillingness or inability to equalize economic and social inequities at a national level, real redistribution of resources that have an impact on health, which requires larger changes in legislation and economic policy.31 Further, knowledge about groups with a more disadvantageous health situation should have implication for resource allocation in the health care system to prevent social inequalities in access to high value health services.32,33 Having knowledge about how health is distributed among the population generate understanding of the etiology of poor physical health and mental distress. Our data suggest that over the past four decades, living conditions have become more unfairly distributed in Norwegian society.

- The absolute inequalities in self-rated health and mental distress have not been reduced but have been stable for men and women aged 30–80 years old since the 1980s.

- Relative inequalities in self-rated health and mental distress have increased during the last four decades. The exception is relative inequalities for men and women aged 60–80.

- There was no difference between men and women regarding the relative inequalities in self-rated health and mental distress.

- In the age group 30–59 years, both men and women of the lowest educational level were more than three times more likely to experience poor self-rated health and mental distress compared with those of the highest educational level.

- Despite political effort to reduce health inequalities, health inequalities have not been reduced in the Norwegian society.
